result.abstractText: In lithium-ion batteries, the bulk solvation structure of the electrolyte is a major determinant of the physical and electrochemical properties of the cell, for example, conductivity, viscosity, salt dissociation and subsequent reactivity, the electrochemical stability window (and thus solid electrolyte interphase formation), and the composition of the electrochemical double layer<sup>1-3</sup>. However, elucidation of this structure at an atomic level of detail has been challenging to accomplish via a purely experimental approach. Here we combine machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations<sup>4-16</sup>, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, electrochemical data<sup>3,17-20</sup> and quantum-chemical calculations to reveal previously unstudied multi-Li<sup>+</sup> complexes without bound anions that are uniquely facile for reduction. This insight explains the success of empirically chosen ethylene-carbonate-containing solvent mixtures and provides a foundation for the rational design of improved electrolytes. Furthermore, our machine-learning force-field-based lithium-ion-battery electrolyte simulations accurately reproduce a wide range of condensed-phase experiments<sup>3,21-24</sup>, despite being parameterized to only quantum-chemical gas-phase cluster calculations, and hence provide a compelling demonstration that machine-learning force-field-based models developed from first principles can robustly represent a complex chemical system to atomic resolution.

result.abstractText: Molecular Hessians, the second derivatives of the potential energy, are fundamental to many workflows in computational chemistry. Usually, accurate Hessians are computationally expensive to calculate and scale poorly with system size, whether computed using quantum chemistry methods or machine learning interatomic potentials. Here we introduce Hessian Interatomic Potentials (HIPs), a deep learning model that directly predicts Hessians without relying on automatic differentiation or finite differences. To do so, we construct SE(3)-equivariant, symmetric Hessians from irreducible representation (irrep) features up to degree l = 2, computed by a graph neural network. HIP Hessians are one to two orders of magnitude faster, more accurate, more memory efficient, easier to train and exhibit favorable scaling with system size. We validate our predictions across a wide range of downstream tasks, demonstrating consistently superior performance in transition state search, geometry optimization, zero-point energy corrections and vibrational analysis. We open source the HIP code and model weights.

result.abstractText: Electrode-electrolyte interphases (EEIs) govern battery performance, yet the interplay between their chemical composition and spatial organization remains challenging to resolve. Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) provides rich 3D chemical depth profiles of these interfaces, yet conventional analyses simplify the complexity by collapsing the data into 1D depth profiles or 2D maps, obscuring critical spatial features. Here, we apply a machine-learning-based approach directly to 3D TOF-SIMS depth profiles, leveraging their full spatial and chemical richness to investigate the interphase structure and chemistry more comprehensively than conventional analyses. Principal component analysis (PCA) identifies fragments that dominate chemical heterogeneity across the EEI, reveals correlated and anticorrelated spatial distributions, and enables direct comparison of average interphase chemistry and chemical variability. Building on this, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) resolve stratified structures and fine-scale spatial interphase variations. Finally, applying PCA to fragment-specific thickness maps enables comparison of interphase thickness heterogeneity and identifies the chemical species responsible for local thickness variations. Together, the approach creates a generalized framework for extracting chemically and spatially meaningful information from complex TOF-SIMS datasets, linking interphase chemistry to electrochemical behavior and guiding the design of uniform interphases for advanced battery systems.

result.abstractText: Asymmetric C-H borylation provides direct access to enantioenriched organoboron compounds. Predictive catalyst design for this reaction class remains challenging, as stereocontrol arises from coupled interactions among catalyst, substrate, and product structures. Moreover, mechanistic knowledge is dispersed across the literature. Here we report a machine-learning framework for predicting enantioselectivity in iridium-catalyzed asymmetric C-H borylation that bridges molecular graphs and chemical literature. A unified dataset comprising 800 literature-reported reactions was constructed for this reaction class. The model combines a multi-entity three-dimensional graph encoder for catalyst, substrate, and product with temperature-aware kinetic treatment, and a large-language-model prior module that extracts atom-resolved mechanistic annotations from primary publications. On a scaffold-based held-out test set, the STEREO-Lit (Spatial Three-Entity Reaction Encoder Literature) model achieves strong predictive performance, outperforming conventional machine-learning baselines and a geometry-grounded control. Perturbation studies further show that literature-derived semantic annotations contribute chemically meaningful, site-specific information rather than merely increasing model capacity. The trained model was subsequently applied to explore a reaction space of about 100 000 catalyst-substrate combinations and identify promising high-improvement candidates, several of which were supported by DFT calculations. The framework couples multi-entity 3D encoding with literature-derived priors, and remains predictive when training data are limited to a few hundred reactions.

result.abstractText: Boron dipyrromethene (BODIPY) dyes are widely recognized for their strong visible-light absorption, high fluorescence, and structural modularity. Beyond fluorescence, molecular engineering can redirect their photoexcited states toward distinct photochemical pathways, expanding their utility in photomedicine and materials chemistry. This Spotlight examines BODIPY photochemistry from this excited-state perspective and connects recent advances in phototheranostics and photopolymerization. In phototherapy, BODIPY excited states can be directed toward triplet-state energy transfer for singlet-oxygen generation, photoinduced electron transfer to form radicals and biomolecular redox modulation, or nonradiative relaxation for photothermal and photoacoustic applications. The same photochemical principles extend to polymer synthesis, where electron transfer with co-initiators or direct photoinduced bond cleavage supports visible-light photoredox catalysis, photobase generation, and Type I photoinitiation. These pathways have been used in applications ranging from panchromatic photocuring to hydrogel formation, holographic patterning, and 3D printing. Overall, BODIPYs provide programmable photoactive platforms whose functions depend on how molecular structure and the local environment distribute excitation energy among competing pathways. Across these applications, excited-state energies, redox properties, and bond dissociation energies provide complementary parameters for directing BODIPY photochemistry. Emerging quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) and machine-learning approaches may further complement these mechanistic design principles by enabling prediction of BODIPY photophysical and photosensitization behavior from molecular structure.
